stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Highway engineers in one state compared cracking on roads surfaced with a new rubber-modified asphalt against roads surfaced with conventional asphalt. After eight years, the rubber-modified roads showed about 40 percent less cracking. However, because of how construction contracts were awarded, most of the rubber-modified roads were in the state's southern counties. Those counties go through far fewer freeze-thaw cycles each winter than the northern counties, and freeze-thaw cycles are a major cause of pavement cracking. The lower cracking rate on the rubber-modified roads therefore ______
choices: may reflect the milder southern climate rather than any advantage of the new asphalt.
shows that the new asphalt is no more durable than the conventional asphalt is.
proves that the new asphalt would resist cracking equally well in any region.
indicates that freeze-thaw cycles have little effect on how pavement cracks.
explanation: The flaw is a confound: the new asphalt was mostly laid where winters are mild, and mild winters by themselves mean less cracking. So you can't tell whether the asphalt or the climate caused the difference. Choice A says the result may come from the climate, and that's as far as the evidence goes.

B.why: You treated the confound as proof of the opposite result. The climate difference only makes the comparison uncertain. It doesn't show that the new asphalt performs no better.

C.why: You took a result from mostly mild-winter roads and applied it to every region. The passage gives you no data on harsh climates, and the confound means even the mild-climate result is unclear.

D.why: The passage says freeze-thaw cycles are a major cause of cracking. This choice reverses that.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Some musicologists argue that nineteenth-century violinists played slow movements much faster than violinists do today. As evidence, they point to wax-cylinder recordings made around 1900 by elderly players who trained in the 1850s. Historian Ruth Okonjo urges caution, however. A typical cylinder could hold only about two to four minutes of sound, so performers often had to finish a movement within that limit or cut it short. Given this constraint, the brisk tempos on the cylinders ______
choices: show that these players actually preferred slower tempos than violinists today.
might not accurately reflect the tempos these players chose in live concerts.
demonstrate that recording length had no influence on how the players performed.
reveal which slow movements were most popular with audiences of the 1850s.
explanation: The complication is the time limit of the medium. Players may have sped up to fit the cylinder, so the recorded tempos may not match how they really played. Choice B says only that the recordings might be misleading, and that's what Okonjo's point supports.

A.why: You swung to a firm conclusion in the other direction. The time limit makes the recordings unreliable, but it doesn't show that these players preferred slower tempos.

C.why: Okonjo's whole point is that the time limit may have shaped the performances. This choice says the opposite.

D.why: Audience preferences never come up. The passage is about whether the recordings show real performance tempos, not which pieces were popular.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: In 2019, managers stocked Lake Marren with yellow perch, a fish that feeds on zooplankton. By the following summer, the lake's zooplankton density had fallen by more than half, and some ecologists attributed the drop to the perch. That same summer, though, surface water in the lake was the warmest on record. Prolonged heat can cut zooplankton numbers by lowering the oxygen in the water. Because of this, the decline in zooplankton ______
choices: was caused by the record heat rather than by feeding from the stocked perch.
proves that stocking perch will reduce zooplankton in any lake where it occurs.
can't be confidently attributed to the perch, since the heat may also have played a role.
suggests that water temperature has little effect on zooplankton populations.
explanation: Two possible causes happened at the same time: the new perch and a record heat wave. The passage gives a way the heat could reduce zooplankton but doesn't show that it did. So the evidence can't settle what caused the decline, which is what choice C says.

A.why: You treated a possible cause as the proven cause. The heat is raised only as an alternative explanation, so it makes the perch explanation uncertain without ruling it out.

B.why: You stretched one confounded result from one lake to every lake. The study can't even establish what happened in Lake Marren.

D.why: The passage says prolonged heat can cut zooplankton numbers. This choice denies the mechanism the text describes.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: To learn whether a traditional verb ending still survives in a coastal fishing region, a linguist recorded hour-long interviews with forty residents. The ending appeared in fewer than 3 percent of the relevant verbs. Yet the residents knew they were being recorded by a university researcher, and many sociolinguists have found that speakers in formal, recorded settings tend to move toward standard forms. The low rate of the traditional ending in the interviews therefore ______
choices: shows that the ending has nearly vanished from the region's everyday speech.
proves that residents use the ending more with strangers than with neighbors.
reveals that most residents in the region had studied at the university.
may understate how often residents use the ending in ordinary conversation.
explanation: The flaw is the setting: people who know a researcher is recording them tend to switch toward standard speech. So the interviews may have captured less of the traditional ending than residents normally use. Choice D says the low rate may be an undercount.

A.why: You accepted the measured rate as the true everyday rate, which is exactly what the complication calls into question. The interview data can't tell you how often residents use the ending at home.

B.why: This reverses the direction of the effect. The passage suggests speakers move away from nonstandard forms in formal settings with outsiders, not toward them.

C.why: The university is mentioned only as the researcher's employer. Nothing in the passage is about the residents' education.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: When a software firm let staff decide whether to work from home, the employees who chose remote work went on to close about 15 percent more support tickets per week than those who stayed in the office. Company leaders cited the figure as evidence that remote work boosts productivity. Labor economist Daniel Ferreira noted, however, that employees who opt into remote arrangements are often those who already work well without supervision. Therefore, the difference in ticket counts ______
choices: indicates that remote work lowered productivity for employees at the firm.
might not show that remote work itself made the employees more productive.
proves that every employee at the firm would close more tickets from home.
confirms that the firm assigned employees to remote work at random.
explanation: The flaw is self-selection: the employees picked their own group, and Ferreira suggests the strongest workers may be the ones who chose remote work. That means the gap could reflect who was in each group rather than where they worked. Choice B is the cautious conclusion this supports.

A.why: You turned doubt into a firm opposite claim. Self-selection makes the boost uncertain, but nothing shows that remote work hurt productivity.

C.why: You applied the result from self-selected volunteers to every employee, with the word 'every' as the giveaway. The passage suggests the volunteers may not be typical.

D.why: The passage says staff decided for themselves whether to work from home, so the groups were not assigned at random.
